topics.title: Growth and development: an open-ended story

learn.hook: A neem tree can keep growing for centuries, but you stop growing taller by your early twenties. Plants have a superpower: meristems that never retire.
points: Development is the sum of growth and differentiation, from the zygote to senescence. A seed germinates under favourable conditions and develops into a seedling and a mature plant.
Development is controlled by intrinsic factors (genetic, and intracellular chemicals such as plant growth regulators) and extrinsic factors (light, temperature, water, oxygen, nutrition).

Growth is an irreversible, permanent increase in size of an organ, its parts or even a single cell. It is generally accompanied by metabolic processes (anabolic and catabolic) that use energy. Example: expansion of a leaf.

Plant growth is generally indeterminate: plants retain the capacity for unlimited growth throughout life because of meristems, whose cells divide and self-perpetuate. New cells are always being added: the open form of growth.

Root and shoot apical meristems cause primary growth (elongation along the axis). In dicots and gymnosperms, lateral meristems, the vascular cambium and cork cambium, appear later and cause secondary growth (increase in girth).

example.q: Classify the growth caused by (a) the shoot apical meristem and (b) the vascular cambium.
steps: Apical meristems increase length along the axis: primary growth.
Vascular cambium is a lateral meristem that increases girth: secondary growth.

learn.reallife: Teak trees in Madhya Pradesh and Kerala thicken year after year because their vascular cambium keeps adding wood, which is why mature teak is valuable timber.

topics.title: Measuring growth and the phases of growth

learn.hook: A single maize root tip can make more than 17,500 new cells every hour. A watermelon cell can swell up to 3,50,000 times. Both are growth, measured differently.
points: At the cellular level, growth is mainly an increase in protoplasm. Since this is hard to measure, we measure quantities proportional to it: fresh weight, dry weight, length, area, volume and cell number.
One maize root apical meristem can give more than 17,500 new cells per hour (growth as cell number). Watermelon cells may increase in size up to 3,50,000 times (growth as cell size).
Pollen tube growth is measured as length; growth of a dorsiventral leaf as increase in surface area.
Meristematic phase: constantly dividing cells at root and shoot apices, rich in protoplasm with large nuclei; thin, primary cellulose walls with abundant plasmodesmata.

Elongation phase (just behind the meristem): increased vacuolation, cell enlargement and new wall deposition. Maturation phase (further from the apex): cells reach maximal size in wall thickening and protoplasmic modifications.

example.q: A maize root apical meristem makes 17,500 cells per hour. How many cells does it make in 4 hours?
steps: Cells per hour = 17,500.

learn.reallife: Crop scientists at ICAR measure wheat growth by plant height, leaf area and dry weight to compare varieties in field trials.

learn.hook: A cricket score growing 6 runs every over is arithmetic. A WhatsApp forward doubling every hour is geometric. Plant growth can follow either pattern.
points: Growth rate is the increase in growth per unit time.

Arithmetic growth: after mitosis, only one daughter cell keeps dividing; the other differentiates. A root elongating at a constant rate gives a linear curve: Lt = L₀ + rt (Lt = length at time t, L₀ = length at time zero, r = growth rate).

Geometric growth: both daughter cells keep dividing. Growth is slow at first (lag phase), then rapid and exponential (log phase), then slows as nutrients become limited (stationary phase), giving a sigmoid (S) curve, typical of organisms in natural environments.

Exponential growth: W₁ = W₀eʳᵗ, where W₁ is final size, W₀ initial size, r the relative growth rate (efficiency index), t time and e the base of natural logarithms. Final size depends on initial size.

Absolute growth rate: total growth per unit time. Relative growth rate: growth per unit time per unit initial size. Example: leaf A grows from 5 to 10 cm² and leaf B from 50 to 55 cm²: same absolute growth (5 cm²), but A has a relative rate of 100% and B only 10%.

example.q: A root is 4 cm long and grows arithmetically at 0.5 cm per day. Find its length after 6 days.
steps: Use Lt = L₀ + rt.
L₀ = 4 cm, r = 0.5 cm/day, t = 6 days.

learn.reallife: Bacterial cultures in Indian biotech labs and populations of crop pests both show S-shaped growth: slow, then explosive, then levelling off.

topics.title: Conditions for growth; differentiation, dedifferentiation and redifferentiation

learn.hook: A xylem cell sacrifices its own living contents to become a water pipe. Some mature cells can even 'turn back the clock' and divide again.
points: Conditions for growth: water (cell enlargement needs it; turgidity aids extension growth; it is the medium for enzymes), oxygen (releases metabolic energy), nutrients (macro and micro elements for protoplasm and energy), an optimum temperature range, and environmental signals such as light and gravity.

Differentiation: cells from apical meristems and cambium mature to perform specific functions, with changes in walls and protoplasm. E.g. tracheary elements lose their protoplasm and develop strong, elastic lignocellulosic secondary walls to carry water under tension.
Dedifferentiation: living differentiated cells that had lost the capacity to divide regain it, e.g. formation of interfascicular cambium and cork cambium from parenchyma.
Redifferentiation: cells produced by dedifferentiated tissues lose the capacity to divide again and mature to perform specific functions (e.g. secondary xylem, secondary phloem, cork).

Differentiation in plants is open: cells from the same meristem mature differently depending on location, e.g. cells pushed away from the root apical meristem become root-cap cells, while those pushed to the periphery become epidermis.

example.q: Classify each: (a) parenchyma forming interfascicular cambium; (b) cambium-derived cells maturing into secondary xylem; (c) meristem cells becoming tracheids.
steps: (a) A mature cell regaining division: dedifferentiation.
(b) Products of dedifferentiated tissue maturing: redifferentiation.
(c) Meristem cells maturing into specialised cells: differentiation.

learn.reallife: Plant tissue culture labs in India, such as those producing banana and sugarcane plantlets, make parenchyma cells dedifferentiate into callus and then redifferentiate into shoots and roots.

learn.hook: A coriander seedling's first leaves are broad and round, but later leaves are feathery. Same plant, different leaf designs.
points: Development includes all changes an organism goes through in its life cycle, from germination of the seed to senescence.
The sequence involves cell division, growth, differentiation and maturation of cells leading to mature tissues and organs, and finally senescence.
Plasticity is the ability of plants to follow different developmental pathways in response to the environment or phase of life, forming different kinds of structures.
Heterophylly due to life phase: juvenile and mature leaves differ in shape in cotton, coriander and larkspur. Heterophylly due to environment: buttercup forms different leaves in air and in water.

Development (growth plus differentiation) is controlled by intrinsic factors (genes, PGRs) and extrinsic factors (environment). (Photoperiodism, vernalisation and seed dormancy are not part of this rationalised chapter.)

example.q: Buttercup leaves under water are finely divided, while those in air are broader. Is this developmental or environmental heterophylly?
steps: Both leaf types can be on the same plant at the same stage.
The difference is caused by growing in water versus air.
So it is heterophylly due to environment.
example.answer: Environmental heterophylly, an example of plasticity.

learn.reallife: Coriander (dhania) in every Indian kitchen garden shows heterophylly: the first leaves are rounded, later leaves are finely divided.

topics.title: Plant growth regulators: nature and discovery

learn.hook: One discovery began with 'foolish' rice seedlings in Japan that grew absurdly tall. Another began with ripe oranges that made stored bananas ripen faster.
points: PGRs are small, simple molecules of diverse chemistry: indole compounds (indole-3-acetic acid, IAA), adenine derivatives (N⁶-furfurylamino purine, kinetin), carotenoid derivatives (abscisic acid, ABA), terpenes (gibberellic acid, GA₃) and gases (ethylene, C₂H₄).

Growth promoters (cell division, enlargement, pattern formation, tropic growth, flowering, fruiting, seed formation): auxins, gibberellins, cytokinins. Growth inhibitors (responses to wounds and stress, dormancy, abscission): abscisic acid. Ethylene can fit either group but is largely an inhibitor.

Auxin: Charles and Francis Darwin saw canary grass coleoptiles bend towards unilateral light (phototropism) and found the tip was the site of a transmittable influence. F.W. Went isolated auxin from oat coleoptile tips.

Gibberellin: E. Kurosawa found that sterile filtrates of the fungus Gibberella fujikuroi, which causes 'bakanae' (foolish seedling) disease of rice, produced the symptoms in uninfected rice seedlings; the active substance was gibberellic acid. Cytokinin: Skoog and co-workers found tobacco callus grew only with extra supplements; Skoog and Miller crystallised kinetin. Kinetin came from autoclaved herring sperm DNA; zeatin was later isolated from corn kernels and coconut milk.

ABA: in the mid-1960s, inhibitor-B, abscission II and dormin were found to be chemically identical and named abscisic acid. Ethylene: Cousins confirmed that ripened oranges release a volatile substance that hastened ripening of stored unripe bananas; it was identified as ethylene.

example.q: Classify these PGRs by chemical nature: IAA, kinetin, ABA, GA₃, ethylene.
steps: IAA: indole compound.
Kinetin: adenine derivative.
ABA: carotenoid derivative.
GA₃: terpene.
Ethylene: gas.
example.answer: Indole, adenine derivative, carotenoid derivative, terpene, gas.

learn.reallife: Indian fruit sellers often keep a ripe banana or mango with unripe fruit to speed ripening, the same ethylene effect Cousins observed with oranges and bananas.

learn.hook: Tea gardens in Assam and Darjeeling are pruned regularly so the bushes grow sideways into flat 'plucking tables'. The trick works by removing the auxin source.
points: Auxins (Greek auxein, to grow) were first isolated from human urine. Natural auxins: IAA and IBA (indole butyric acid). Synthetic: NAA (naphthalene acetic acid) and 2,4-D (2,4-dichlorophenoxyacetic acid). They are produced at growing apices of stems and roots and migrate to regions of action.

Uses: initiate rooting in stem cuttings (plant propagation); promote flowering, e.g. in pineapple; prevent fruit and leaf drop at early stages but promote abscission of older mature leaves and fruits.
Apical dominance: the growing apical bud inhibits growth of lateral (axillary) buds. Decapitation (removing the shoot tip) lets lateral buds grow; used in tea plantations and hedge-making.
Auxins induce parthenocarpy, e.g. in tomatoes.
Auxins are used as herbicides: 2,4-D kills dicot weeds but does not affect mature monocots, so it is used for weed-free lawns. Auxin also controls xylem differentiation and helps in cell division.

example.q: Why does 2,4-D sprayed on a lawn kill broad-leaved weeds but not the grass?
steps: 2,4-D is a synthetic auxin used as a herbicide.
It kills dicotyledonous weeds.
It does not affect mature monocots such as lawn grasses.
example.answer: It is selective: it kills dicot weeds but spares mature monocot grass.

learn.reallife: Nursery owners across India dip stem cuttings of roses and bougainvillea in auxin (IBA/NAA) rooting powder to make them root faster.

learn.hook: Spraying sugarcane with gibberellins can add as much as 20 tonnes per acre to the yield. Sweet results from a hormone.
points: More than 100 gibberellins (GA₁, GA₂, GA₃ ...) are reported from fungi and higher plants; GA₃ (gibberellic acid) was among the first discovered and is the most studied. All GAs are acidic.

Gibberellin uses: increase axis length (longer grape stalks); elongate and improve shape of fruits like apple; delay senescence so fruits stay on the tree longer; speed up malting in brewing; increase sugarcane stem length and yield (up to 20 tonnes per acre); hasten maturity and early seed production in juvenile conifers; promote bolting (internode elongation just before flowering) in beet, cabbage and other rosette plants.
Cytokinins promote cytokinesis. Kinetin, a modified adenine (purine), does not occur naturally in plants; zeatin is a natural cytokinin from corn kernels and coconut milk.
Natural cytokinins are made where rapid cell division occurs: root apices, developing shoot buds, young fruits.

Cytokinin effects: production of new leaves and chloroplasts, lateral shoot growth, adventitious shoot formation; overcoming apical dominance; promoting nutrient mobilisation, which delays leaf senescence.

example.q: A farmer wants cabbage to bolt for seed production and wants a stored leaf to stay green longer. Which PGR suits each?
steps: Bolting (internode elongation before flowering) is promoted by gibberellins.
Delay of leaf senescence through nutrient mobilisation is a cytokinin effect.
example.answer: Gibberellins for bolting; cytokinins to delay leaf senescence.

learn.reallife: Sugarcane growers in Uttar Pradesh and Maharashtra may use gibberellins to lengthen stems, and table-grape farmers in Nashik use GA₃ to lengthen bunches and enlarge berries.

quiz.q: Cytokinins delay leaf senescence by:
quiz.explain: Nutrients are moved into the leaf, keeping it active.

quiz.q: Natural cytokinins are synthesised in:
quiz.explain: They form where cells divide rapidly.
quiz.mistake: Thinks they come from senescent parts
options: Regions of rapid cell division such as root apices and young fruits

quiz.q: Which PGR helps overcome apical dominance?
quiz.explain: Cytokinins promote lateral shoot growth.
quiz.mistake: Picks auxin, which causes apical dominance

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Gibberellins promote bolting in cabbage and beet. Reason (R): Gibberellins are used to speed up malting in the brewing industry.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both are true uses of gibberellins, but malting in brewing has nothing to do with why cabbage bolts; bolting is due to GA-induced internode elongation just before flowering.
quiz.mistake: Assumes two true statements must be cause and effect

teach.ask: Gappu asks how grape farmers get long bunches and why some leaves stay green longer. Explain gibberellins and cytokinins!
teach.praise: Chirp! GAs stretch stems and fruits; cytokinins make new shoots and keep leaves young!
teach.nudge: Good! Give one use of gibberellins and one effect of cytokinins.

learn.hook: One gas ripens mangoes and pineapples in Indian markets; another hormone tells plants to shut their stomata when drought hits. Meet ethylene and ABA.
points: Ethylene is a simple gaseous PGR made in large amounts by senescing tissues and ripening fruits. In dicot seedlings it causes horizontal growth, swelling of the axis and apical hook formation (the triple response).

Ethylene promotes senescence and abscission of leaves and flowers; is highly effective in fruit ripening, raising the respiration rate (respiratory climacteric); breaks seed and bud dormancy (germination of peanut, sprouting of potato tubers); promotes rapid internode and petiole elongation in deep-water rice; promotes root growth and root hairs; initiates flowering and synchronises fruit-set in pineapple; induces flowering in mango.

Ethephon is the most widely used source of ethylene; in water it is absorbed and releases ethylene slowly. It hastens ripening in tomatoes and apples, accelerates abscission (thinning of cotton, cherry, walnut) and promotes female flowers in cucumber.
Abscisic acid (ABA) regulates abscission and dormancy; it is a general inhibitor of growth and metabolism, and inhibits seed germination.

ABA stimulates stomatal closure and increases tolerance to stresses, so it is the stress hormone. It is important in seed development, maturation and dormancy, helping seeds withstand desiccation. In most situations ABA is an antagonist of GAs.

example.q: Why do farmers use ethephon on cucumber crops?
steps: Ethephon releases ethylene slowly inside the plant.
Ethylene promotes female flowers in cucumbers.
More female flowers mean more fruits.
example.answer: To increase female flowers and hence the yield.

learn.reallife: Fruit traders in India are allowed to use ethylene gas (not calcium carbide, which is banned by FSSAI) in ripening chambers for mangoes and bananas.

games.title: Ethylene and ABA check
items: It is the most used ethylene source.
Ethylene breaks dormancy and sprouts potato tubers.
It breaks seed and bud dormancy.
ABA usually acts together with GAs in the same direction.
ABA is mostly an antagonist of GAs.
Ethylene promotes elongation of deep-water rice.

quiz.q: The rise in respiration rate during fruit ripening caused by ethylene is called:
quiz.explain: Ethylene enhances respiration in ripening fruits.

quiz.q: ABA is called the stress hormone because it:
quiz.explain: It helps plants cope with drought and other stresses.
options: Closes stomata and increases tolerance to stresses

quiz.q: The most widely used source of ethylene in agriculture is:
quiz.explain: Ethephon releases ethylene in the plant.

quiz.q: Which PGR induces flowering in mango?
quiz.explain: Ethylene induces flowering in mango and pineapple.

quiz.q: ABA in most situations acts as an antagonist to:
quiz.explain: ABA opposes GA effects, e.g. in germination.

quiz.q: Ethylene promotes rapid internode elongation in:
quiz.explain: This keeps leaves above water.

quiz.q: Horizontal growth of seedlings, swelling of the axis and apical hook formation in dicot seedlings are effects of:
quiz.explain: Together these are the triple response to ethylene.

quiz.q: Assertion (A): ABA helps seeds survive desiccation. Reason (R): ABA induces seed dormancy.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true; by inducing dormancy, ABA helps seeds withstand desiccation.
quiz.mistake: Does not link dormancy with surviving drying

teach.ask: Gappu sees mangoes ripening in a chamber and a wilting plant closing its stomata. Explain ethylene and ABA!
teach.praise: Tweet! Ethylene ripens and drops; ABA shuts stomata and keeps seeds asleep. A busy pair!
teach.nudge: Good! Name two effects of ethylene and two of ABA.

topics.title: Interaction of PGRs and practical applications

learn.hook: Plant hormones rarely act alone. Like players in a cricket team, they combine, compete or cover for each other.
points: Every phase of growth, differentiation and development is influenced by one PGR or another. Their roles may be complementary or antagonistic, individualistic or synergistic.
Many events involve interaction of more than one PGR: dormancy in seeds and buds, abscission, senescence and apical dominance.
Apical dominance: auxin from the apex maintains it, while cytokinins help overcome it. Dormancy: ABA maintains it, while GAs and ethylene can break it.
PGRs are only one kind of intrinsic control; along with genomic control and extrinsic factors they regulate growth and development.

Practical choices: rooting of cuttings (auxin, IBA/NAA); weed control in lawns (2,4-D); seedless tomato (auxin); longer grape stalks, malting, sugarcane yield, bolting (GAs); fruit ripening, female flowers in cucumber, flowering in pineapple and mango (ethylene/ethephon); stomatal closure under drought (ABA); delay leaf senescence (cytokinin).

example.q: Pick a PGR for each: (a) speed up malting, (b) make stored tomatoes ripen evenly, (c) root a hibiscus cutting.
steps: (a) Malting is speeded up by GA₃.
(b) Ripening is hastened by ethylene, released from ethephon.
(c) Rooting of cuttings is initiated by auxins such as IBA or NAA.

learn.reallife: Horticulture departments in states like Maharashtra and Himachal train farmers to use the right PGR at the right dose, because wrong use can damage crops or leave residues.

quiz.q: A gardener wants seedless tomatoes. Which PGR should be used?
quiz.explain: Auxins induce parthenocarpy in tomatoes.
quiz.mistake: Picks ethylene because it relates to fruits

quiz.q: To increase the number of female flowers in cucumber, a farmer should use:
quiz.explain: Ethylene from ethephon promotes female flowers.

quiz.q: To help a plant survive drought by closing stomata, the relevant PGR is:
quiz.explain: ABA triggers stomatal closure.

quiz.q: PGRs that work together to enhance an effect are said to act:
quiz.explain: Synergy means combined enhancement.

quiz.q: Which event involves interaction of more than one PGR?
quiz.explain: Auxin and cytokinin interact in apical dominance.

quiz.q: To lengthen grape stalks, growers spray:
quiz.explain: GAs increase axis length.

quiz.q: Which PGR is used to hasten ripening and to thin cotton by accelerating abscission?
quiz.explain: Ethylene hastens ripening and abscission.

quiz.q: Assertion (A): ABA and gibberellins often have opposite effects. Reason (R): In most situations, ABA acts as an antagonist to GAs.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true; R states the antagonism described in A.
quiz.mistake: Does not see that R explains A

teach.ask: Gappu is a new farmer with a list of problems: rooting cuttings, ripening fruits, drought and seedless tomatoes. Prescribe the right PGR for each!
teach.praise: Chirp! Auxin roots, ethylene ripens, ABA saves water, GA stretches. Farm doctor Gappu!
teach.nudge: Good! Which PGR would you use for rooting and which for ripening?
